content: 1. Follow up with the patient in 4 weeks. If there is no anemia, provide iron and folate supplementation for 3 months. 2. If the mother is severely ill or separated from the baby, teach her to express breast milk every 3 hours. Assist her in expressing milk if necessary and ensure the baby receives the mother’s milk. Help her establish or re-establish breastfeeding as soon as possible. 3. In the case of a stillborn or deceased baby, provide supportive care. Inform the parents promptly about the baby’s death. Show the baby to the mother and allow her to hold the baby if culturally appropriate. Offer the parents and family private time with the baby for as long as they need. Discuss the events leading to the death and possible causes. Advise the mother on breast care and counsel her on appropriate family planning methods. Record the event and complete the perinatal death certificate. 4. During childbirth and immediate postpartum care, address any problems immediately. Ensure all preventive measures are provided before discharge. Check records for RPR status. If RPR is positive, treat the woman and her partner with benzathine penicillin and treat the newborn as necessary. 5. Check tetanus toxoid immunization status and administer it if due. Provide mebendazole once every 6 months. Supply 3 months of iron and counsel on adherence. Note that vitamin A is not recommended for postpartum women to prevent maternal and infant morbidity and mortality. 6. Ask if the woman and baby are sleeping under insecticide-treated bed nets and encourage their use. Advise on postpartum care, including hygiene, nutrition, and family planning. Counsel on breastfeeding, safer sex practices, and routine postpartum visits. Discuss danger signs and how to prepare for emergencies. 7. Record all treatments given and findings in home-based records. Check HIV status in records. If HIV-infected, support adherence to antiretroviral therapy and treat the newborn as needed. Measure hemoglobin levels if possible and assess for pallor. 8. If severe anemia (hemoglobin <7 g/dL) is detected during early labor or postpartum, refer the patient urgently to a hospital. If in late labor, monitor intensively, minimize blood loss, and refer urgently after delivery. For moderate anemia (hemoglobin 7–11 g/dL), check hemoglobin after 3 days, provide a double dose of iron for 3 months, and follow up in 4 weeks. 9. Advise postpartum women to always have someone nearby for the first 24 hours to respond to any changes in condition. Emphasize the importance of rest, sleep, and hygiene to prevent infections. Teach proper handwashing, perineal care, and safe disposal of used pads. Advise against inserting anything into the vagina and avoiding sexual intercourse until the perineal wound heals. 10. Counsel on nutrition, encouraging the woman to eat a variety of healthy foods to regain strength. Reassure her that normal foods will not harm the breastfeeding baby. Address any cultural food taboos and involve family members in ensuring the woman eats well and avoids strenuous physical work. 11. Discuss family planning and birth spacing. Explain that a woman can become pregnant as early as 4 weeks postpartum if not exclusively breastfeeding. Encourage early consideration of family planning methods and provide counseling on available options. 12. For breastfeeding women, explain that lactational amenorrhea is effective only if the woman is exclusively breastfeeding, is less than 6 months postpartum, and has not resumed menstruation. Offer additional family planning methods if needed. 13. Advise on when to return for routine postnatal care. The first contact should occur within 24 hours after childbirth, the second on day 3, and the third between days 7 and 14. Encourage the woman to bring her partner or family member to at least one visit. 14. Educate on danger signs that require immediate medical attention, such as excessive vaginal bleeding, convulsions, severe headache with blurred vision, difficulty breathing, fever with weakness, severe abdominal pain, or signs of deep vein thrombosis. 15. For home deliveries, ensure emergency arrangements are in place, including transportation and essential supplies. Follow labor and delivery procedures, maintain universal precautions, and provide supportive care. 16. Stay with the mother for the first two hours after delivery of the placenta and examine her before leaving. Ensure someone stays with her for the first 24 hours. Advise on postpartum care, nutrition, and family planning. 17. For the newborn, stay until the baby has had the first breastfeed and assist with proper positioning and attachment. Examine the baby, provide immunizations if possible, and advise on newborn care and danger signs. 18. Conduct postpartum examinations up to 6 weeks after delivery. Record findings and address any complications. Ensure the uterus is well-contracted, there is no excessive bleeding, and the mother is feeling well. 19. Counsel the woman and her family on what to watch for and when to seek care. Provide guidance on postpartum hygiene, nutrition, and the importance of birth spacing and family planning.
